rules.rule: A command reports what it did, in a line or a few
rules.detail: Like gh, git and aws. Explanation lives in the guide, the walkthrough, --help and the glossary, never in output.

rules.rule: An action prints one line
rules.detail: Past tense, naming the thing: 'Created endpoint acme.demo.bob', "Mail sent (number 42 in acme.demo.alice's inbox)". It does not print what another command already shows; it does print an identifier the person can get nowhere else.

rules.rule: Minimal by default, in text and in JSON alike; --detail gives the fuller answer in both
rules.detail: A command's usual answer is the least that answers the question, and --json prints that same least as an object. --detail asks for more: in text, 'label: value' lines after the usual line; with --json, a fuller object that contains the usual one. The fuller object's extra keys are the text's extra labels, in lower case with underscores ('holds endpoint' is holds_endpoint), so the two can be checked against each other. A program that needs the fuller object asks for it, as a person does. An MCP tool takes detail the same way. --wide is the same idea for a table: more columns, and it may pass 80 columns. --detail is one option with one meaning on every command of both tools, so nobody has to learn which commands have it: where a command has nothing more to say, --detail prints what it prints without it. Every --detail and --wide form that does add something is written out in this specification.

rules.rule: A list is a plain table
rules.detail: A header row in capitals, two spaces between columns, no borders. A repeated leading value may be left blank. --wide adds columns. An empty list is one sentence.

rules.rule: One thing is a list of 'label: value' lines
rules.detail: The labels are the JSON field names.

rules.rule: Status is one line
rules.detail: '<what>: <state>'. Everything behind it is in doctor.

rules.rule: An error is one line on stderr, and at most one hint
rules.detail: 'error: <what failed>', then 'hint: <a command to run>' when there is one. No hint on success, and no 'next step' lines.

rules.rule: --json prints one object
rules.detail: Always an object, never a bare array: a list is {"endpoints": [...]}. It is the same object the matching MCP tool returns as its structured result. Field names are the glossary's words. Both are produced by one implementation. One policy in both tools: it is indented when standard output is a terminal and one compact line when standard output is a pipe or a file, as gh and aws do. An error object follows the same policy. The specification shows the indented form.

rules.rule: A wrong command line gets one error line in a fixed form, and one hint
rules.detail: A missing argument: 'error: mash send needs <address>'. A bad value: 'error: --kind must be one of blocker, question, task, result, fyi' or 'error: --reply-to must be a whole number'. Two things that cannot go together: 'error: mash send takes the message text or --file, not both'. An option that does not exist: 'error: unknown flag --x', with no hint. Every other wrong command line has the command's own help as its hint: 'hint: mash send --help'. Exit 2, and nothing is attempted.

rules.rule: --help has one layout, generated from this specification
rules.detail: For a command, in this order: the one-line description; 'Usage:' and the synopsis; 'Examples:'; 'Arguments:'; 'Options:'; 'Global options:'. Nothing else, 80 columns. For the tool itself: its one-line description, then one heading per group in the specification's order ('Everyday:', 'Setup:', 'Integration:', 'Raw SAP:' for mash; 'Mesh:', 'Endpoints:', 'Owners:' for mashctl) with each command and its one-line description indented beneath, then 'Global options:'. Help is never written by hand beside the specification.

rules.rule: Times read the way a person says them
rules.detail: '10s ago', '2m ago', '1h 12m'. Anything under a second, or in the future because two clocks disagree, is 'just now'. --json carries the exact time.

rules.rule: Text read from a file or standard input loses one trailing newline
rules.detail: As the shell's own $(...) does. Nothing else in the text is changed.

rules.rule: One exit rule, the same in both tools
rules.detail: 0 it worked, 1 it failed, 2 the command line was wrong and nothing was attempted. This holds for every command of mash and mashctl. A command that needs another code is named here as an exception; none is left implicit. There is one exception today: mash hook exits 0 whatever happens, so that a bad configuration or a failed check never fails the session that runs it. No command exits with a code above 2. status and doctor are not exceptions: they exit 1 when they found a problem (a warning alone is 0, or 1 with --strict), as a failure does. A command that did part of its work exits 1, says what is left, and is safe to run again.

rules.rule: Both doctors work the same way
rules.detail: mash doctor and mashctl doctor print every row every time, each marked ok, warn, FAIL or skip; a row that cannot run because an earlier one failed is skip, with what it needs. 'checks' in --json always lists every row, whatever failed. After the rows come one blank line and a count ('No problems.', '1 problem, 1 warning.'). A hint is a command of ours that fixes the problem, or there is no hint and the row's own words say what is wrong. A doctor prints at most one hint. It is never a command that only checks, and never one that replaces credentials, moves a folder or changes permissions unless the doctor found exactly the condition that command fixes. With no problem, the first warning that has a command that fixes it gets one hint. Exit 1 when there is a problem; warnings alone exit 0, or 1 with --strict. A server row shows the address as configured.

rules.rule: status and doctor report, they do not fail
rules.detail: Their lines go to stdout whatever they find, and they exit 1 when they found a problem. Any hint still goes to stderr.

rules.rule: Where a hint is printed
rules.detail: At a shell, every 'hint:' line goes to stderr, whichever stream the rest went to: after an error, after status, after doctor's count. The case pages show the hint beneath the text it follows, for reading; a case marked stdout means its lines other than the hint. In an MCP tool's text block the hint is the last line.

rules.rule: The server not answering reads the same everywhere
rules.detail: 'error: the server did not answer: tls://host:4222' and 'hint: mash doctor' (or mashctl doctor), exit 1. Two more server failures have fixed words: 'the server's certificate is not trusted: <address>' and 'the server did not offer TLS: <address>'.

rules.rule: Missing credentials read the same in every everyday command
rules.detail: When the chosen endpoint's creds file is not where the configuration says: 'error: acme.demo.bob has no credentials here: ~/.config/mash/acme.demo.bob.creds is missing' and 'hint: mash doctor', exit 1, from send, inbox, read and who alike; status says the same as its reason (reason_code creds_missing) and doctor in its creds row. Never the operating system's own wording. A recipient that takes no mail reads 'error: <address> is suspended or was deleted; nothing was sent', hint 'mash who', exit 1; never the server's wording. The sender cannot tell the two apart: all it sees is that no stream took the message, and a recipient deleted while the sender's directory cache still lists it looks the same; a marker in the directory record that tells them apart is planned for 0.6.0. When the set-aside file <address>.creds.deleted is present, send, inbox, read and who say 'error: <address>: this endpoint was deleted; its address cannot be used again' with 'hint: mash doctor', as mash status does.

rules.rule: A case written in brackets is a description
rules.detail: A case whose whole text stands in round brackets, such as '(the same JSON as --json ...)', describes the output in words; it is not a form to match byte for byte, and the conformance test skips it. The JSON example beside it shows the shape. A part of a case that varies from run to run (a key id, a cause as the server gave it) is named in that command's notes, with the words that stand before and after it; a test matches everything else byte for byte and nothing more loosely than the notes say.

rules.rule: Having no endpoint reads the same in every mash command
rules.detail: Three wordings, by where it is asked. At a shell with none installed: 'error: no endpoint is installed here', no hint, exit 1. At a shell with several installed and none chosen: 'error: more than one endpoint is installed here: <addresses>' and 'hint: mash <command> --endpoint <the first, alphabetically>', exit 2. As an MCP tool in a session with none named: 'No endpoint is chosen for this session.' and 'hint: start the session with MASH_ENDPOINT=<address>'.

rules.rule: --json when a command fails
rules.detail: Prints {"error": ..., "hint": ...} on stdout and nothing on stderr, with the same exit code.

rules.rule: Every command that changes the mesh or this machine's setup takes --dry-run
rules.detail: It prints the usual line with 'Would' in front and changes nothing; with --json the object is the one the real run would print, with "dry_run": true. In the --json of every command that takes --dry-run (mashctl's changing commands, limits apply included, and mash join) the dry_run key is always present: false when the run is real (and mashctl init adds would_change, null unless it is a dry run). Sending a message is not such a change and has no --dry-run.

rules.rule: help is also a command
rules.detail: 'mash help' and 'mash help send' print exactly what 'mash --help' and 'mash send --help' print, as git, kubectl and gh do. The same for mashctl.

rules.rule: Every setting three ways
rules.detail: A flag, then an environment variable, then config.json. The flag wins.

rules.rule: One spelling
rules.detail: An address is owner.group.name everywhere. NATS's and SAP's things keep NATS's and SAP's names. The same thing has the same column heading and the same field name in every command.

rules.rule: A prefix selects, the way a domain name does
rules.detail: Where a command takes a prefix, acme means everything under acme, acme.demo everything under acme.demo, and a full address that one endpoint. acme.* is accepted and means acme. There is no other pattern matching.

rules.rule: Options go anywhere after the tool's name
rules.detail: Every option, global or the command's own, is accepted before or after the command and its arguments, as with kubectl and gh. Help and documentation always write them last: mash status --endpoint acme.demo.alice.

rules.rule: A sender's words are always marked as the sender's
rules.detail: Wherever mash prints a message's text in full, every line starts with '> ' and control characters are escaped, at a shell and in an MCP tool alike. It reads as quoted mail does to a person, and it shows an agent where data from someone else begins and ends. A table's MESSAGE column holds the sender's words too.

rules.rule: Encryption can be turned off in one way only, and it says so every time
rules.detail: Both tools talk to the server over TLS. The one way to turn that off is the environment variable MASH_DANGEROUSLY_SKIP_NATS_ENCRYPTION=1. There is no flag and no configuration-file key for it: this is the one setting that cannot be given three ways, so that it cannot be left on in a file and forgotten. While it is set, every command of both tools, errors included, first prints, on stderr: 'warning: no encryption to the server (MASH_DANGEROUSLY_SKIP_NATS_ENCRYPTION)'. The older names, MASH_INSECURE_PLAINTEXT and the key insecure_plaintext, are refused with an error naming the new one.

rules.rule: Only a destructive command asks
rules.detail: It asks you to type the address, and --yes skips the question.

rules.rule: Eighty columns, and color only on a terminal
rules.detail: --wide may be wider. NO_COLOR is honored.

rules.rule: In --json, one name for one fact
rules.detail: A yes-or-no fact has one name in every command of both tools: online is a boolean wherever it appears (mash who, mash status, mashctl endpoint list and show, mashctl status), never ready, ok or state for the same fact; an endpoint's suspended state is its own boolean, suspended. ready stays the name of "mail works for this endpoint" and "the server works" (mash status and mashctl status, which was ok). A count is named as a count: endpoint_count, online_count, wake_count. An unset field is null: never "" and never left out, so a command's keys are the same on every run. An empty list is [] and an empty map is {}. A list's key is plural: capabilities, not capability. The one exception is mash who --json, which follows ADR 0049 as amended by ADR 0184 (who JSON fields are added, never renamed or removed) and so keeps capability; it prints every field for every endpoint, an unset role, host or description as null and no capability as []. A doctor row's state (ok, warn, fail, skip) is a different fact and keeps its name.

words.meaning: The whole: every endpoint and all their mail.
One mailbox on the mesh, used by one agent, tool or person.
The first part of an address: a namespace. In 0.5.6 a mesh has one owner, named at mashctl init. Several owners per mesh are planned for 0.6.0.
The second part: endpoints an owner keeps together.
The third part: this one endpoint.
owner.group.name, for example acme.demo.bob.
One item of mail.
The messages an endpoint has received.
Whether something is holding the endpoint open right now.
Proven to come from the address it names.
What sort of message it is, and whether it should interrupt.
One text file that lets a machine use an endpoint: server address, certificate authority, creds.
A NATS server: a way in to the mesh.
The NATS unit users belong to, and which signs them.
The private half of a key pair.
The half that can be shared.
A statement signed by the account that a public key is a given user.
One text file, in the style of a PEM file, holding a user JWT and its seed.
An endpoint as SAP sees it, and SAP's live operations.
SAP's optional signature on a message, which mash requires.

coming_in_0_6_0.change: mash prompt becomes mash sap prompt
coming_in_0_6_0.meaning: And the MCP tool reply moves with it.
mashctl owner create, list and delete arrive. Mail between owners becomes a designed case, under policy.
Planned, with no release named. Who may send to whom. mash ships open; narrowing is a choice.
An endpoint can ask to join and be approved by an administrator or by policy.

coming_in_0_6_0.change: The MCP revision and how a session is woken
coming_in_0_6_0.meaning: Planned for 0.6.0: a study of the MCP Events extension as the way to wake a session. Channels stay until then.

setup.name: install.sh
setup.what: Finds the machine's type, downloads mash and mashctl from the same release, checks each against the release's checksums, and against the release's signed record too when gh 2.102.0 or newer is there to do it, printing one line when that check passes: 'Verified the release attestation for bogworks/mash v0.5.6', checked against the commit the release tag points to (with no gh, a gh that does not run, a gh whose version it cannot read, or one older than 2.102.0, it prints one warning line on stderr that says which, such as 'warning: gh not found: checked checksums only, not verified'; if the check fails it prints 'error: the release failed verification; nothing was installed' on stderr, installs nothing and exits 1; if it cannot read that commit it prints 'error: could not read the commit of bogworks/mash v0.5.6; nothing was installed' on stderr, installs nothing and exits 1), puts them in ~/.local/bin unless MASH_INSTALL_DIR names another folder, and prints one line for each, with the path it actually used: 'Installed mash v0.5.6 (3f9a41c) in ~/.local/bin'. It asks nothing and needs no sudo. If that folder is not on the PATH it says so in one line. If the folder, or a folder above it, can be written by its group or by other users, it installs nothing and prints one refusal that names every such folder, nearest first, and one fix: chmod go-w with each folder in single quotes, then run it again.

setup.name: mash-local-nats-setup.sh
setup.what: For a NATS server on this machine. It works on Linux and on macOS, where many developers will first try mash. First install nats-server (version 2.10.7 or newer) and the nats command. nats-server comes from your package manager. The nats command has no Debian or Ubuntu package: on those, get it from the natscli GitHub release. Homebrew has both. The script also needs openssl, to make the server's certificate. If nats-server is not on the PATH, it also looks in /usr/sbin, /usr/local/sbin and /sbin, as Debian's package installs it there; it uses one found there only if it and its folder are owned by root and not writable by others, and says which one it uses. It names anything missing, says where to get it, and stops. It does not need nsc. If port 4222 is already taken, as it is where a packaged nats-server runs as a system service, the script leaves that service alone, uses the next free port and says which. It asks one question, the owner's name, reading it from the terminal; --owner NAME answers it on the command line and nothing is asked, which is the form an agent or a script uses, since it has no terminal. It makes a server that only this machine can reach, with encryption on, starts it as your own user, and writes the setup file. That is its whole scope: a join file made against it works only on this machine. Two machines need a server both can reach, with a certificate that covers its address; in 0.5.6 that is a NATS server you run yourself, which mashctl init takes from a setup file (docs/install.md). Planned for 0.6.0: a script option for a reachable address and certificate. Everything goes in ~/mash-nats unless --dir names another folder. Its last line is the next command, with the path it actually wrote: 'mashctl init --config ~/mash-nats/mash-setup.yaml' by default. Guides and skills take that path from the script's output, never from memory. The NATS account it makes is named after the owner; the system account keeps NATS's own name, SYSTEM. The server runs as your own user's process, not as a system service, so it does not come back after a reboot: run the script again with --start to start it (it never creates anything then), --stop to stop it, or --remove to remove it. When --start finds its server process already running, it first checks that the server answers: if it does, it says 'already running'; if the process is alive but the server does not answer, it stops with an error and changes nothing (it does not kill or restart), and the hint is to run --stop, then --start. After --remove it prints two lines: that mashctl's folder still points at the server just removed, and how to set up again (a new configuration folder, or moving the old one aside).

setup.name: <release base>
setup.what: Every address in these commands is written from the release's own setting, so a fork or a mirror points at itself; in the project's own releases it is the address shown here. One printed line carries an address: the plugin's 'mash is not installed' line, which carries the address shown here, written into the launcher (mash hook).

setup.name: For an agent
setup.what: The setup skill does not pipe a download into a shell. It downloads each script, checks it against the release's checksums, shows the person what it is about to run, and runs it after a yes.
